content: Endometriosis is a condition characterized by the presence of endometrial tissue, including glands and stroma, outside the uterine cavity. This condition is estrogen-dependent and primarily affects women during their reproductive years. Progesterone receptor modulators (PRMs) have been proposed as a treatment option for endometriosis due to their antiproliferative effects on the endometrium. The primary objective of this research was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of PRMs, particularly in terms of pain relief, compared to other treatments, placebo, or no treatment in women of reproductive age with endometriosis. The study included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed the effects of PRMs on symptomatic endometriosis. Pain relief and side effects were the primary outcomes measured. A total of 10 RCTs involving 960 women were included in the analysis. These trials compared various PRMs, including mifepristone, asoprisnil, ulipristal, and gestrinone, against placebo, other PRMs, or alternative treatments such as danazol, gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) analogues, or leuprolide acetate. The quality of evidence ranged from high to very low, with limitations including risk of bias, imprecision, and indirectness. Mifepristone versus placebo: One study compared mifepristone to placebo and found that, at three months, women in the mifepristone group experienced significantly lower rates of dysmenorrhea (odds ratio [OR] 0.08, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.04 to 0.17; moderate-quality evidence). This suggests that if 40% of women taking placebo experience dysmenorrhea, only 3% to 10% of women taking mifepristone would experience it. Additionally, the mifepristone group had lower rates of dyspareunia (OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.51; low-quality evidence). However, side effects were more common in the mifepristone group, with nearly 90% experiencing amenorrhea and 24% reporting hot flushes, compared to only 1% in the placebo group (high-quality evidence). There was insufficient evidence to determine differences in rates of nausea, vomiting, or fatigue. Mifepristone dose comparisons: Two studies compared different doses of mifepristone but found insufficient evidence to determine differences in effectiveness or safety. However, subgroup analysis suggested that the 2.5 mg dose may be less effective than the 5 mg or 10 mg doses for treating dysmenorrhea and dyspareunia. Gestrinone comparisons: One study compared gestrinone to danazol, and another compared gestrinone to leuprolide acetate. Evidence was insufficient to determine differences in pain relief, dysmenorrhea, or dyspareunia between gestrinone and danazol (very low-quality evidence). However, the gestrinone group had higher rates of hirsutism (OR 2.63, 95% CI 1.60 to 4.32; very low-quality evidence) and lower rates of decreased breast size (OR 0.62, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.98; low-quality evidence). There was insufficient evidence to determine differences in rates of hot flushes or acne. When comparing gestrinone to leuprolide acetate, the mean dysmenorrhea score was higher in the gestrinone group (mean difference [MD] 0.35 points, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.58; low-quality evidence), while the mean dyspareunia score was lower (MD -0.33 points, 95% CI -0.62 to -0.04; low-quality evidence). The gestrinone group had lower rates of amenorrhea (OR 0.04, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.38; low-quality evidence) and hot flushes (OR 0.20, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.63; low-quality evidence) but higher rates of spotting or bleeding (OR 22.92, 95% CI 2.64 to 198.66; low-quality evidence). There was insufficient evidence to determine differences in effectiveness or safety between different doses of gestrinone. Asoprisnil versus placebo: One study involving 130 participants compared asoprisnil to placebo but did not provide data suitable for analysis. Ulipristal versus leuprolide acetate: One study involving 38 participants compared ulipristal to leuprolide acetate but did not provide data suitable for analysis. Conclusions: Moderate-quality evidence indicates that mifepristone is effective in relieving dysmenorrhea in women with endometriosis, while low-quality evidence suggests it may also relieve dyspareunia. However, common side effects include amenorrhea and hot flushes. Data on the optimal dosage of mifepristone were inconclusive, though the 2.5 mg dose may be less effective than higher doses. There was insufficient evidence to draw firm conclusions about the safety and effectiveness of other PRMs, including asoprisnil, ulipristal, and gestrinone.
